highlights:
# AWS 二度上调 GPU 预留算力价格，7 月起再涨约 20%

 2026-07-15 14:33:43 分享到 

亚马逊云科技（AWS）再次上调了 GPU 预留算力的价格。据多家外媒报道，自 2026 年 7 月 1 日起，AWS 面向机器学习的 EC2 Capacity Blocks（算力预留）价格上调约 20%。这已是 AWS 今年内的第二次提价——今年 1 月曾先行上调约 15%，两次叠加之下，AI 训练与推理的算力预留成本明显抬升。

## 涨价覆盖哪些实例 

本次调整集中在 AWS 最强的英伟达 GPU 实例系列，包括 P6-B300、P6-B200、P5、P5e、P5en 与 P4de 等。按官方口径，基于 Blackwell 架构的 P6-B300 实例达到每 GPU 每小时约 14.04 美元，基于 H100 的 P5 实例在美国区域调整为约 5.191 美元；其余 EC2 产品价格保持不变。AWS 解释称，算力预留价格会"根据供需周期性调整"。 

## 涨价背后的供需与投入 

这轮提价发生在企业对 GPU 算力需求持续高涨之际。AWS 2026 年第一季度营收同比增长约 28%，达到约 376 亿美元；亚马逊 2026 年在 AI 基础设施上的资本开支承诺约为 2000 亿美元。在高端 GPU 供不应求的背景下，云厂商拥有了较强的定价能力。也有云成本分析人士认为，这类调整更接近"提价的政策决定"，而未必全然由即时供需驱动。对以年初价格制定预算的团队而言，两次连续上调意味着成本假设需要重新校准。

results.title: Together, Runpod and Nebius capitalize on AWS GPU shortages to lure AI startups
highlights:
Together AI, Runpod, and Nebius have positioned themselves as alternative cloud providers for AI startups that need serious compute power amid reported GPU shortages affecting larger hyperscalers like AWS.

Together AI operates as an NVIDIA Cloud Partner, offering H100 clusters at $6.79 per hour on-demand or $4.55 per hour per GPU on reserved pricing. The company was reportedly in talks to raise funding at a $7.5 billion valuation as of March 2026.

Runpod supports more than 30 different GPU types globally and charges on a per-second billing model.

Nebius partnered with NVIDIA on March 11, 2026, to deploy more than 5 gigawatts of NVIDIA systems by the end of 2030. The company is investing approximately $2.3 billion to construct UK-based capacity targeting 65 megawatts by 2027, using NVIDIA’s Blackwell Ultra infrastructure.

results.title: AWS Charges $6.88/Hour for an H100, CoreWeave Charges $2.40 - The Markup Is Not Profit, It's Idle Infrastructure
highlights:
- AWS charges $6.88/hour for H100 GPUs, 2-5x higher than specialized clouds like CoreWeave CRWV-4.05% ($2.40/hour), driven by infrastructure costs and idle capacity.

- GPU hardware costs represent only 5-13% of total expenses; $5.9M GB200 racks require $2.4M+ for power/cooling infrastructure alone.

- Hyperscalers maintain 30-50% GPU utilization to meet enterprise SLAs, tripling effective costs compared to specialized clouds with 70-80% utilization.

- AWS/Azure add $0.08-$0.12/GB egress fees, while specialized providers compete on total cost with zero egress charges and lower markup.

- Price gaps may narrow if hyperscalers improve utilization or if GB200's $81,944/GPU rack economics reduce infrastructure costs per unit.

A single NVIDIA NVDA+4.06% H100 costs $25,000–$40,000 to buy. Rent one on a specialized GPU cloud like CoreWeave CRWV-4.05% or Lambda Labs, and the price is roughly $1.50 to $3.30 per GPU-hour. Go to AWS, and it's $6.88. Azure charges $12.29. Google Cloud's 8-GPU H100 instance runs about $80 to $90 per hour - about $10 to $11 per GPU-hour.

...

Here's where the markup makes structural sense. Most AI clusters run at 30% to 50% GPU utilization, according to infrastructure operators. Over 75% of organizations report GPU utilization below 70% at peak load. That means when you pay $6.88 per GPU-hour on AWS, you're paying for a chip that is idle roughly half the time.

Hyperscalers build capacity for peak demand, not average demand. They can't say no to an enterprise customer who needs 1,000 GPUs tomorrow. That means they have to keep a massive pool of idle hardware ready - and the cost of that idle capacity is baked into the per-hour price. If utilization is 50%, the effective cost doubles. At 30%, it more than triples.

Specialized GPU clouds have a different cost structure. They don't need the enterprise SLA buffer. They don't maintain the same level of guaranteed capacity. Their utilization rates are higher because they serve a different customer base - AI startups, researchers, and developers who can tolerate some scheduling friction in exchange for lower prices. But even at the specialized cloud's higher utilization, spot pricing for H100 has fallen to $1.20/hr, suggesting there's still excess capacity in the market.

...

The per-GPU-hour price is not the full cost on the hyperscaler. AWS charges egress fees - data transfer out of the cloud - at roughly $0.08–$0.12 per GB. For training jobs that move large datasets in and out, that adds a second layer of cost on top of the GPU rental. At the scale of a serious AI training run, egress fees can add thousands of dollars per month.

CoreWeave and some specialized providers advertise zero egress fees. That's not charity - it's a structural difference. They're smaller networks with less diversified services, so they compete on total cost rather than building a fee stack across multiple product lines.

## Who's Actually Making Money?

AWS recently raised GPU prices by 15%, with instances jumping from $34.61 to $39.80/hr. That's roughly $3,700 more per month per instance. Meanwhile, H100 one-year rental contracts rose nearly 40% from a low of $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026, according to SemiAnalysis's rental price index.

Both markets are getting more expensive. But the hyperscaler's markup over the wholesale rental market is widening, not narrowing.

The reason is structural. Hyperscalers are not just selling GPU hours. They're selling the enterprise guarantee - security compliance, data residency, multi-region redundancy, and the trust that your infrastructure won't disappear because a GPU startup ran out of funding. That trust has a price.

But the trust premium is not free. At Azure's price of $12.29 per GPU-hour for an H100, you're paying five times the specialized cloud's on-demand rate. That gap is too wide to be explained by infrastructure costs alone. Part of it is margin. Part of it is the cost of carrying idle capacity. Part of it is the hyperscaler's need to fund the next wave of data center buildout from current GPU revenue.

...

That would pressure hyperscalers to either justify their markup or compress it.

## B200 rental pricing just got a clearer real-time signal

### The number to watch

B200 compute is now $4.22 per hour, down from $6.11 per hour in a 31% drop. For now, that is one of the clearest near-term signals that GPU pricing power may be softening. If flagship compute rents are slipping, scarcity alone may be less protective than it once was.

...

Its compute forward curves for Nvidia B200, H200, and A100 chips are now live, giving readers a view of implied future rental pricing over time rather than only a spot snapshot. The more important question is shifting from whether AI demand remains strong to what buyers will actually pay for compute in coming weeks and months.

results.title: RunPod vs Vast.ai: Which GPU Cloud Wins in 2026?
highlights:
RunPod vs Vast.ai is a choice between reliable value and rock-bottom price. RunPod is a low-cost GPU cloud with dedicated Pods and serverless inference. Vast.ai is a marketplace where independent hosts rent out spare GPUs at the lowest prices.

Both let you rent modern GPUs by the hour far cheaper than the big clouds. But they differ on reliability and features. RunPod offers a consistent platform; Vast.ai offers the lowest raw price.

...

## RunPod vs. Vast.ai: Side-by-Side

| Dimension | RunPod | Vast.ai |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | Dedicated low-cost GPU cloud with serverless | Marketplace of community-hosted GPUs |
| Price | Low, consistent hourly rates (H100 ~$2.89/hr) | Often the lowest, but varies by host |
| Reliability | Consistent, platform-managed | Varies by individual host |
| Serverless inference | Yes, scales to zero when idle | No native serverless |
| Ease of use | Polished, beginner-friendly | More hands-on, host-dependent |
| Best for | Reliable, flexible GPU work | Squeezing out the lowest price |
| Bottom line | Pick it for reliable value plus serverless | Pick it for the cheapest raw GPUs |

...

The core difference is a managed platform versus a marketplace. RunPod runs its own consistent GPU cloud with Pods and serverless inference. Vast.ai connects you to independent hosts renting spare GPUs, which can be cheaper but less uniform.

...

## RunPod vs Vast.ai Pricing: Which Is Cheaper?

Vast.ai usually wins on raw price. Because independent hosts compete to rent out spare GPUs, prices can dip below dedicated clouds, which is its main appeal.

RunPod is still very cheap and more consistent, with H100 Pods around $2.89 per hour and RTX 4090s around $0.69. Its prices do not swing with individual hosts.

So Vast.ai can be cheaper per hour, but RunPod offers predictable pricing plus serverless billing that pays nothing while idle.

Vast.ai often has the lower raw price; RunPod offers predictable rates plus serverless that bills only for active inference.

results.title: Kalshi Puts GPU Prices on Trial: $6.11 to $4.22 Says AI Compute May Be Easing
highlights:
- Kalshi introduces a forward curve for AI GPU pricing, tracking B200/H200/A100 hourly rental costs to create a transparent term structure.

- The platform competes with CME/ICE by offering real-time data, but faces challenges in establishing benchmark authority against established exchanges.

- Success depends on third-party adoption for hedging and pricing workflows, not just speculative trading, to solidify its market influence.

- Currently serving as an early cost signal, Kalshi's curve remains unproven as a standard until commercial usage surpasses novelty-driven activity.

...

A recent B200 compute-rate drop from $6.11 to $4.22 an hour in a month matters because Kalshi is now packaging that kind of spot movement into a broader forward signal. The platform builds its curve from weekly and monthly chip prices and shows the implied future cost of renting one hour of B200, H200, and A100 capacity. That makes the product more than a one-off spot read; it creates a visible term structure for AI compute.

...

The counterargument is that price discovery is not the same as benchmark ownership. CME and ICE have announced their own compute futures products, and both bring existing client relationships, balance-sheet strength, and established trading ecosystems.

Settlement is the key pressure point. Kalshi resolves contracts using real-time data from Ornn, so the benchmark is only as authoritative as Ornn's coverage and the market's willingness to accept it. If large renters and hyperscalers do not start quoting the index, Kalshi can win attention without winning the standard.

...

For now, Kalshi looks more useful as an early warning signal than as a final verdict. The recent declining B200 rates matter because lower or softening compute pricing could ease AI input costs even if it pressures the GPU-scarcity trade. Buyers can now watch a live forward signal before that softness shows up clearly in margins.

results.title: The Economics of LLM Inference: Cloud vs. On-Premise Hardware
highlights:
GPU compute in 2026 isn't a single market with one price — it's four separate channels with meaningfully different pricing: hyperscaler clouds (AWS, Azure, GCP, Oracle), specialist "neocloud" providers (CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius, Crusoe), long-tail marketplaces (Vast.ai, RunPod, Thunder Compute, Hyperstack), and direct hardware purchase (Thunder Compute — AI GPU Rental Market Trends). The spread between the cheapest and most expensive channel for the same hardware is enormous.

## Real cloud rental pricing across the spread

As of mid-to-late 2026, on-demand H100 rental ranges from roughly $1.38–$1.49/hour on marketplace and boutique providers up to $11.68–$12.29/hour on hyperscaler on-demand instances — nearly a 9x spread for functionally the same GPU (CloudZero — Cloud GPU Pricing Comparison 2026). Neocloud providers sit in between and represent the more commonly quoted "real" market rate: median on-demand H100 pricing runs about $4.17/hour on dedicated neoclouds versus about $7.89/hour on hyperscalers — an 89% hyperscaler premium (Thunder Compute — AI GPU Rental Market Trends).

Provider-specific numbers make the spread concrete:

| Provider | H100 on-demand rate |
| --- | --- |
| Lambda | $3.99/hr |
| CoreWeave | $4.76/hr |
| Azure (hyperscaler) | $12.29/hr |

(Thunder Compute)

CoreWeave's rate runs roughly 1.6x Crusoe's and 1.8x Lambda's — but that premium buys guaranteed multi-year capacity and service-level agreements backed by a contract base reported at $66.8 billion (Thunder Compute). For newer Blackwell-generation hardware, Lambda currently lists the lowest B200 rate at $6.69/hour and Crusoe the lowest H200 at $4.29/hour (Thunder Compute).

## Reserved and spot pricing change the math further

On-demand isn't the only lever. Reserved contracts cut on-demand rates by up to 60% — roughly 25% savings on a one-year term and about 45% over a three-year commitment. Spot instances rent for about half of on-demand pricing but carry the risk that the provider can reclaim that capacity with little warning (CloudZero — Cloud GPU Pricing Comparison 2026).

Warning

Spot-to-on-demand discounts have compressed hard since mid-2026 — the savings gap has narrowed noticeably from where it stood even a year earlier, even though H100 spot prices had fallen as much as 88% between January 2024 and September 2025 as supply caught up with demand (CloudZero). Don't plan a cost model around historical spot discounts without checking current spreads — they move.

Market dynamics have also been volatile in the other direction recently: contract pricing for H100 and H200 GPUs climbed roughly 40% between October 2025 and March 2026 as HBM3e memory costs collided with surging demand (MarkTechPost — Best GPU Neoclouds 2026). In August 2026, CoreWeave's CEO noted the company had contracted A100 GPUs all the way out to 2029 at full pricing — a signal that large buyers are locking in capacity years ahead rather than betting on falling prices.
